html:
Traits are Rust's answer to interfaces. Generics are its answer to templates. Together they give you polymorphism with zero runtime cost — but they also generate the error messages that Rust is famous for. This module teaches you to read them.

Defining a trait

A trait is a set of guarantees. Any function that takes impl Summary can rely on all of them and knows nothing else about the concrete type.

Generic functions

T: PartialOrd + Copy is a bound: T must support comparison and copying. Without it, item > max does not compile because the compiler cannot assume anything about T.

Monomorphisation, and its cost

Generic functions are compiled once per concrete type. largest::<i32> and largest::<f64> are two separate functions in the binary. That is why generics are as fast as hand-written code, and why they increase binary size and compile time.

Use dyn Trait (below) instead when binary size or compile time dominates, or when the set of types is open.

impl Trait in argument position

Sugar for fn notify<T: Summary>(item: &T). Use it for one generic parameter; use explicit <T> when you need two parameters of the same type.

impl Trait in return position

The concrete type (Filter<Take<RangeFrom<u32>>, ...>) is unnameable, so impl Trait lets you return it without boxing. This is the standard way to return iterators and futures.

Trait objects: dyn Trait

impl Trait / <T: Trait> dyn Trait
Dispatch static (inlined, monomorphised) dynamic (vtable)
Cost per call zero one indirect call
Binary size grows per type one
Heterogeneous collections no yes
Compile time higher lower

Rule of thumb: generics by default; dyn when you need a collection of mixed types, a plugin boundary, or you are fighting compile time.

Object safety

Not every trait can become dyn Trait. A trait is object-safe only if it has no generic methods, no Self: Sized requirements, and no associated constants or methods returning Self.

Fix: add where Self: Sized to the offending method so it is excluded from the vtable.

Common standard traits

Trait Method Gives you
Clone .clone() explicit deep copy
Copy — implicit copy semantics
Debug {:?} developer output
Display {} user output
PartialEq / Eq == comparison (Eq = total equality)
PartialOrd / Ord <, .sort() ordering
Hash — usable as HashMap key
Default T::default() zero/empty value
From / Into .into() infallible conversion
TryFrom / TryInto .try_into() fallible conversion
AsRef / Borrow .as_ref() cheap re-interpretation
Iterator for, .map() iteration
Deref *x, auto-deref smart pointer behaviour
Drop — destructor
Send / Sync — thread safety markers

Deriving

Derive is a procedural macro that writes the impl. For Hash + Eq pairs, both are needed for HashMap keys. Ord requires PartialOrd + Eq.

Implementing Display and Error

Once Display + Debug + Error exist, the type works with ?, Box<dyn Error>, anyhow, thiserror, and every logging crate.

Supertraits

Send + Sync supertraits are the standard way to say "this abstraction is usable from async tasks".

Associated types vs generic parameters

Use an associated type when there is exactly one sensible choice per implementation (Item). Use a generic parameter when a type could sensibly implement it several ways (Add<i32> and Add<f64>).

Static dispatch across a plugin boundary

Trait objects at runtime: a plugin registry

This is how routers, CLI subcommands and migration runners are structured internally.

Blanket implementations

Powerful and dangerous: a blanket impl blocks anyone else from implementing Describe for their own type. The standard library uses this for impl<T: Display> ToString for T.

Extension traits

Adding methods to a type you do not own:

This is how itertools, tower, axum and sqlx add ergonomics without touching upstream types.

Reading generic error messages

The fix is to add Copy (as we did) or to work with &T. Reading these messages: the help: block is usually the correct fix; the note: block explains why.

The Sized bound

?Sized means "may not have a known size at compile time" — required for &str and dyn Trait parameters.

A worked example: a generic repository with a trait object fallback

Exercises

  1. Write trait Area { fn area(&self) -> f64; }, implement it for three shapes, then write fn total(shapes: &[Box<dyn Area>]) -> f64.
  2. Convert total to a generic fn total<A: Area>(shapes: &[A]) -> f64. What can you no longer pass it, and why?
  3. Implement From<&str> for Meters and confirm "5".into() works.
  4. Write an extension trait VecExt adding .second() returning Option<&T>. Apply it to Vec<i32> and Vec<String>.
  5. Take a trait with a method returning Self and make it object-safe using where Self: Sized.
  6. Explain why impl<T: Display> MyTrait for T prevents you from also writing impl MyTrait for MyStruct.
